name: Ringo Corponation Distributed Optic Swarm
description:
The Distributed Optic Swarm is a reconnaissance drone system consisting of twelve semi-autonomous micro-units, each approximately the size of a large insect, capable of independent navigation and collective mesh-coordinated surveillance. Each unit carries a wide-aperture optical sensor, a short-range acoustic pickup, and a minimal onboard processor running RINGO's SWARM coordination firmware. Individually, each drone is limited — its optics are adequate but not exceptional, its battery life is measured in minutes, and its processing is insufficient for complex autonomous behavior. Collectively, the swarm is a different instrument entirely.

The DOS's engineering distinction is RINGO's COLLECTIVE APERTURE protocol, which treats the twelve optical sensors as a single distributed imaging array. By correlating the slightly different perspectives of drones positioned across a space, the system constructs composite imagery of significantly higher resolution and depth than any single unit could produce. It also enables triangulation of sound sources, detection of active electronic emissions through multi-point signal comparison, and the identification of targets occluded from any individual drone's line of sight. The operator interface is a wrist-mounted display and a neural-adjacent earpiece that translates swarm data into a navigable overview — experienced operators describe controlling the DOS as developing a sense of the space rather than watching a feed.

RINGO CORPONATION markets the DOS primarily to investigative and intelligence clients — journalists, corporate intelligence firms, and private investigation agencies. Its civilian positioning keeps it below the threshold of military equipment regulation in most districts, though security forces have pushed repeatedly to have it reclassified. The swarm's small individual signature makes it exceptionally difficult to detect with standard anti-drone countermeasures, which are calibrated for larger units. The DOS is widely used and widely feared by anyone who needs to maintain operational security in GLMZ's layered interior spaces.

specifications.operator_interface: Wrist display unit plus neural-adjacent earpiece
specifications.recharge_time: 22 minutes full swarm via included cradle

tactical_use: Standard deployment involves releasing the swarm through a small opening — ventilation gap, mail slot, partial door breach — and using the collective aperture to map an interior space before physical entry. The acoustic triangulation function identifies personnel positions behind walls and through floors with reasonable accuracy. Electronic emission detection locates active devices — security terminals, communication hardware, powered weapons. In extended operations, swarm units can be staged at relay positions to extend communication range through signal-dead areas. Losing units to anti-drone countermeasures degrades but rarely eliminates capability, making the DOS resilient in hostile environments.
cultural_context: The DOS has a reputation that precedes it in corporate security circles — the discovery of a single swarm unit in a facility is treated as a major security event because the implication is that someone already has a detailed map of the interior. Among investigative journalists and freelance intelligence operatives, the DOS is considered essential equipment, a great equalizer that lets a single operator achieve surveillance coverage that previously required a team. There is a documented subculture of DOS operators who share swarm navigation techniques and COLLECTIVE APERTURE interpretation methods through encrypted forums — RINGO is believed to monitor these forums as a product development intelligence source.
known_users: Investigative journalists operating in restricted corporate zones
story_hooks: A DOS swarm is recovered from inside a sealed corporate server room with its memory intact — the flight logs show it was navigating the space for six hours before the facility went into lockdown, and the imagery it captured includes personnel whose presence in that location is officially impossible.

One of the players' swarm units fails to return after a reconnaissance deployment — days later, it reappears in an unexpected location, suggesting it was captured, examined, and deliberately released, possibly with modifications.

RINGO Corponation pushes a mandatory firmware update that introduces a new feature: anonymous telemetry reporting swarm deployment locations back to RINGO's servers. An operator who reverse-engineers the update brings it to the players, and the question is what RINGO is doing with a real-time map of everywhere their product is being used.

A corporate security firm has developed a new counter-swarm protocol that identifies DOS units by their COLLECTIVE APERTURE communication signature — the players must complete a reconnaissance mission using a DOS against a target that is now specifically hardened against it.

physical_description.visual_profile: Twelve insect-like micro-drones with articulated wings, each resembling a mechanical dragonfly or wasp. Sleek, aerodynamic bodies with forward-swept optical turrets. When docked, they nest in a hexagonal charging cradle the size of a large deck of cards. In flight, individually nearly invisible to the naked eye; as a swarm, they create a barely-perceptible shimmer or haze.
physical_description.dimensions: Individual units: 3.2cm wingspan, 1.1cm body length. Charging cradle: 12cm × 10cm × 4cm. Operator wrist display: 6cm × 4cm. Earpiece: negligible.
physical_description.weight_description: Individual units: 1.4 grams each — feather-light, pocket-portable. Full swarm kit in carrying case: approximately 200 grams. Wrist display adds minimal weight to operator.
physical_description.primary_material: Injection-molded aerospace composite body with carbon-fiber reinforced sections. Transparent polymer optics enclosure. Aluminum or titanium micro-frame for structural integrity.
physical_description.finish: Matte black primary finish on bodies with iridescent bronze or copper anodized accents on sensor housings. Non-reflective to minimize detection. Micro-articulations have a brushed metallic finish.
physical_description.color_scheme: Deep matte black bodies with amber or copper-colored optical sensor turrets. Minimal branding in gunmetal gray. Charging cradle is industrial matte gray with neon orange indicator strips for power status.
physical_description.interface_elements: Each unit has three micro-LED indicators (power, link status, thermal). Wrist display features a 3.5-inch flexible OLED screen with haptic feedback, three physical control buttons, and a USB-C charging port. Earpiece is a thin bone-conduction transducer with capacitive touch surface. Cradle features inductive charging pads and a physical status readout.
distinctive_features: Distributed optical sensor array with visible micro-lens turrets on each unit
Visible mesh-communication antenna filaments along wings
Triangulated acoustic pickup grilles on fuselage
Synchronized LED breathing pattern when docke — all units pulse in unison
Ultra-compact hexagonal charging nest that doubles as transport container
Cradle's neon orange status indicators that glow during active operation
physical_description.manufacturer_markings: RINGO CORPONATION logo (stylized radio wave symbol) on cradle and wrist display. Serial number etched discreetly on individual unit underside. 'DISTRIBUTED OPTIC SWARM' text stamped on charging cradle in 4pt font. Regulatory compliance marks: GLMZ civilian classification, non-military designation.
physical_description.condition_typical: In operation, drones are nearly invisible in flight; operator's attention is on the wrist display, which shows a composite overhead view with depth-mapped targets and acoustic source triangulation. At rest, units are stored in the hexagonal cradle, all LEDs synchronized. Carrying case is reinforced synthetic leather with internal foam compartments, approximately briefcase-sized.
